name: Birhor
lead: Birhor (from Kherwarian bir 'forest' + hōṛ 'person/man') is a Critically Endangered North Munda (Austroasiatic) language spoken by the traditionally semi-nomadic Birhor community across the Chota Nagpur Plateau in Jharkhand, northern Odisha, and Chhattisgarh.[1][2] Within the Kherwarian branch, it is closely related to Mundari, Ho, and Santali.[1]
history: The Birhor community historically comprised two socio-ecological groups: the Uthlu (nomadic hunter-gatherers specializing in monkey-trapping and making chēp rope from bauhinia creeper bark) and the Jaghi (semi-settled cultivators).[1][2] Although the 2011 Census recorded roughly 17,000 ethnic Birhors, active mother-tongue transmission is restricted to fewer than 2,000 speakers due to shift toward Sadri (Nagpuri), Hindi, and Odia.[1][2]
phonology: Like other Kherwarian languages, Birhor exhibits preglottalized/checked word-final stops (/p̚, t̚, c̚, k̚/, realized with glottal closure before pause and voiced intervocalically), a retroflex series (/ʈ, ɖ, ɽ/), and five core vowels (/i, e, a, o, u/).[1][2]
syntax: Birhor has a complex polysynthetic verbal template: Verb Stem + Aspect/Valency + Transitivity/Object Marker + Finite Copula (-a) + Subject Enclitic.[1][2] Nouns distinguish animate and inanimate gender, which controls pronominal agreement on the verb complex.[1]

lessons.title: Lesson 1: 11-Pronoun Number & Inclusivity System
lessons.intro: Birhor distinguishes singular, dual, and plural numbers, plus inclusive and exclusive first-person forms (Anderson 2008: 199–205; Jora 2016).<sup>[1][2]</sup>

quiz.q: How does Birhor distinguish 'you and I (dual inclusive)' from 'someone else and I (dual exclusive)'?
What is the literal etymology of the ethnonym Birhor?

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Verbal Roots & Finite Marker -a
lessons.intro: Declarative finite clauses require the finitizer suffix -a before or after the subject enclitic.<sup>[1][2]</sup>

quiz.q: How does Birhor distinguish transitive past from intransitive past on the verb?
quiz.a: Transitive verbs take -ket̚-/-ked-, whereas intransitive verbs take -en-/-yan-.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Interlinear Glossed Sentences
lessons.intro: Polysynthetic verbal indexing from Anderson (2008) and Jora (2016).<sup>[1][2]</sup>

quiz.q: What is the role of the final -ñ in nū-ket̚-a-ñ?
quiz.a: First-person singular subject enclitic (-ñ < iñ) attached after the finite marker -a.
